title: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
summary: The SOC analyst's day job: triage alerts with four questions, enrich them, investigate logins, endpoints, egress, cloud keys and ransomware precursors, then escalate, write it up and automate safely.
outcomes: Explain how events, alerts and incidents differ and how an alert moves from firing to a documented verdict
Triage an alert with four questions and classify it as true, false or benign true positive, separating severity from priority
Enrich alerts with asset, identity and intel context in Python, and spot shared-IP, CDN, stale-intel and geolocation traps
Investigate impossible travel, MFA push storms, help desk MFA resets, process trees, data egress, cloud key misuse and ransomware precursors
Pivot across data sources, build a UTC timeline and map it to MITRE ATT&CK, labelling inferences as such
Decide when to escalate and write case notes and stakeholder updates that others can act on
Choose what a SOAR playbook should automate and where a human must approve, and judge SOC metrics, burnout risks and access ethics

lessons.title: What a SOC is, and what an analyst does all day

blocks.md:
It is 09:02 on a Tuesday. A detection rule fires: *a laptop in Finance just ran `rundll32.exe` on a file in its Temp folder*. Somebody has to look at that alert, decide within minutes whether it is an attack, and either close it with a reason or raise the alarm. That somebody works in a **SOC** (security operations centre: the team, and often the room, that watches an organisation's security data around the clock and responds to what it finds).

The previous course built the machinery that produces alerts: log pipelines, the SIEM (security information and event management system, which stores logs and runs detection rules over them) and the rules themselves. This course is about the person at the other end of that machinery. It is the day job of many entry-level security roles.

Three words get mixed up constantly, so fix them now, using the definitions in NIST SP 800-61r3 (NIST is the US National Institute of Standards and Technology; SP 800-61 (Special Publication 800-61) is its incident response guide, revision 3 published in April 2025):

- An **event** is "any observable occurrence" involving computing assets: a login attempt, a software update, a web request.
- An **adverse event** is an event "associated with a negative consequence". Many need more analysis before anyone knows what they mean.
- An **incident** is an occurrence that "actually or imminently jeopardizes" the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information or systems, or violates security policy.

An **alert** sits between them: a rule's way of saying *a human should look at this event*. The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) puts it bluntly in its SOC guidance: "Not every alert will be an incident."

A SOC is more than people staring at a queue. The NCSC lists the common functions:

- **Threat intelligence**: what attackers are doing now, including IOCs (indicators of compromise: hashes, IP addresses, domains that mark known attacker activity).
- **Threat hunting**: proactively looking for attackers that no rule caught.
- **Content development**: turning intelligence into detection rules.
- **Engineering**: keeping the tools running and the logs flowing ("plumbing").
- **Incident response or handling**: investigating events to decide whether they are incidents.
- **Incident management**: running a confirmed incident, from communications to technical containment.

Most SOCs split the triage work into levels. In a six-month anthropological study of a corporate SOC (Sathya Chandran Sundaramurthy and colleagues at Kansas State University, presented at SOUPS 2015, the Symposium on Usable Privacy and Security), **Level 1 (L1)** analysts were "the first line of defense", watching the SIEM console in 10-hour shifts; **Level 2 (L2)** analysts mentored them and produced metrics; a separate **incident management** team took the cases L1 escalated for in-depth analysis. Many SOCs call these Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3. The names and boundaries vary from company to company, and many smaller teams have no tiers at all.

The NCSC warns against pigeonholing: keeping analysts on one narrow task "often leads to issues, like triage fatigue, poor job satisfaction and therefore poor security". It recommends rotating analysts through intelligence, rule writing and incident handling.

blocks.title: Where an alert goes inside a SOC

scenes.caption: Endpoints, servers, identity providers and cloud accounts send logs. EDR (endpoint detection and response) agents and the SIEM run rules over them.
A rule matches and an alert lands in the shared queue with a severity, the matching event and whatever context the rule could attach.
A Tier 1 analyst picks it up and triages: is this real, is it expected, how bad could it be? Most alerts end here, closed with a verdict and a note.
If triage cannot rule out an attack, the case goes to Tier 2 for deeper investigation, and from there to incident response if it meets the incident criteria.
Every verdict feeds back to the content team: a rule that keeps producing false positives gets tuned. This loop is what keeps the queue workable.

blocks.md:
**Shifts and handover.** Attacks do not keep office hours, but people must. The NCSC notes that a 24/7 SOC "will require significantly more staff" than a 9 to 5 operation with out-of-hours on-call, and suggests routing high-priority out-of-hours alerts either to an existing 24/7 IT team for first triage or straight to an on-call analyst. Whatever the model, every shift change is a moment where work can fall through the gap.

A good **handover** answers four questions for the next shift: what is still open, what is each case waiting on (and since when), what is the next step and its deadline, and what has changed in the environment (a log source that went silent, a new rule, a planned change window). The script below prints such a note from case records.

blocks.code:
# SYNTHETIC open cases at the end of a night shift
cases = [
    {"id": "C-311", "title": "Impossible travel: ana.silva",
     "status": "waiting", "waiting_on": "user reply (phoned 05:40)",
     "next": "if no reply by 09:00, revoke sessions"},
    {"id": "C-305", "title": "Encoded PowerShell on WEB-PROD-01",
     "status": "escalated", "waiting_on": "IR on-call (paged 04:10)",
     "next": "host isolated 04:05; IR owns it now"},
    {"id": "C-313", "title": "Proxy log source silent since 02:00",
     "status": "open", "waiting_on": "platform team ticket P-88",
     "next": "web alerts are blind until fixed"},
]

def handover(cases, shift="night 2026-11-12/13"):
    lines = [f"HANDOVER {shift}"]
    for c in sorted(cases, key=lambda c: c["status"] != "escalated"):
        lines.append(f"- {c['id']} [{c['status']}] {c['title']}")
        lines.append(f"    waiting on: {c['waiting_on']}")
        lines.append(f"    next step:  {c['next']}")
    return "\n".join(lines)

print(handover(cases))
blocks.caption: handover.py: escalated cases first, then each case's blocker and next step. All data is synthetic.

blocks.md: An alert is a question, not an answer. The analyst's job is to answer it with evidence, record the answer so someone else can check it, and feed what was learned back into the rules.

blocks.question: A rule fires because a user typed the wrong password three times. Using the NIST definitions, what is it so far?
options: An event that may be an adverse event; triage decides whether anything jeopardised systems or data
An incident, because a security rule fired
A false positive, because wrong passwords are normal
Nothing worth recording
blocks.explain: Failed logins are events. Whether they are adverse, and whether they add up to an incident (a password-guessing attack that succeeded, say), is exactly what triage decides. Calling it an incident or a false positive before looking skips the work.

blocks.question: Which handover note is most useful to the next shift?
options: "Quiet night, a few alerts, all handled"
A list of every alert ID closed during the shift
"C-311: waiting on user reply since 05:40; if none by 09:00, revoke sessions. Proxy logs silent since 02:00, ticket P-88"
"Ask me if anything comes up"
blocks.explain: The next shift needs open items, what each is blocked on, the next step with a deadline, and environmental changes such as a dead log source. A list of closed IDs or a vague summary gives them nothing to act on, and the author may be asleep.

lessons.title: The alert lifecycle, and why the queue is not first come, first served

blocks.md:
Every alert goes through the same life, whatever the tool:

1. **Fire**: a rule matches and creates the alert, often opening a ticket automatically (NIST SP 800-61r3 suggests considering exactly that).
2. **Triage**: a quick, structured first look. Is it real, is it expected, how bad could it be?
3. **Investigate**: if triage cannot close it, gather more evidence across data sources.
4. **Escalate or close**: hand it to incident response, or close it with a verdict.
5. **Document**: at every step, write what you saw, what you did and why.

Case management tools (the ticketing systems SOCs use) model this as states. The rules about moving between states are worth enforcing in code, because the shortcut everyone is tempted to take, closing without saying why, is the one that hides attacks.

blocks.caption: lifecycle.py: a tiny case state machine. Every move needs a note; closing needs a verdict.

blocks.code:
refused: closing needs a verdict
closed false_positive 2 moves
blocks.caption: Output: the lazy close is refused; the second close records why the alert was wrong.

blocks.md:
The NCSC asks SOCs to record the actions taken during triage so that periodic quality reviews can check "that alerts (false positive or not) aren't being dismissed without good reason". The note is also how a rule gets better: "dest IP is our CDN; rule lacks CDN allow list" tells the content team exactly what to fix.

Now the queue. Alerts arrive unevenly: a noisy rule, a misconfigured scanner or a real campaign can add hundreds in an hour. NIST SP 800-61r3 is direct about what that means for ordering: "Because of resource limitations, incidents should not be handled on a first-come, first-served basis." The same is true of alerts. The figure shows a synthetic morning in a small SOC.

blocks.title: One morning's alert queue by severity (synthetic)

scenes.caption: 08:00, start of shift after handover: 39 open alerts, mostly low and informational. Two highs are waiting.
10:00: a misconfigured vulnerability scanner trips a port-scan rule over and over. Low alerts jump to 94. Working the queue oldest first would bury the three highs under scanner noise.
Same moment, worked by priority: the three highs are triaged first (two closed, one escalated), mediums next. Lows wait, which is acceptable only because someone is looking at why they spiked.

12:00: one analyst traced the spike to the scanner, the rule now excludes the scanner's address for its scheduled window, and the 80 duplicates were closed together under one note. The queue is workable again.

blocks.prompt: At 10:00 the queue holds 94 low alerts from one port-scan rule and 3 high alerts from three different rules. You have one hour. What do you do first, and what do you do second?
blocks.reveal: First the three highs, by priority (next lessons show how to rank them). Second, spend a few minutes on the *spike itself*: 94 alerts from one rule in two hours is a signal. Either something is scanning your network, or something changed (a new scanner, a broken parser). Find out which, fix the cause, then close the duplicates together with one note. Clicking through 94 alerts one by one is the worst option: slow, mind-numbing, and the one real alert hidden among them gets the same three seconds as the rest.

blocks.md: Allow-listing the scanner fixes the noise but creates a blind spot: an attacker on that address is now invisible to the rule. The NCSC says allow lists must be "strongly object/time bounded" (one address, its scheduled window, an expiry date) "to minimise the risk of perpetual allow listing and the evasion of monitoring".

blocks.question: An analyst tries to close a case with the note "looks fine" and no verdict. Why should the case tool refuse?
options: Because closed cases cannot be reopened
Because without a verdict and a reason, nobody can review the decision or tune the rule, and real attacks dismissed this way are never found
Because every alert must be escalated to Tier 2 before closing
Because notes must be at least 100 characters
blocks.explain: The verdict and the evidence-based reason are what quality review and rule tuning run on. "Looks fine" cannot be checked by anyone, which is exactly how alerts get "dismissed without good reason".

blocks.question: Why does NIST advise against first-come, first-served handling?
options: Because older alerts are usually false positives
Because analysts work faster on new alerts
Because resources are limited and the order of work should follow risk: asset criticality, impact, how far the attack has progressed
Because SIEMs sort alerts randomly
blocks.explain: Ordering by arrival time lets the noisiest source decide what gets looked at. NIST lists risk evaluation factors such as asset criticality, functional and data impact, stage of observed activity and recoverability as the basis for triage and prioritisation.

lessons.title: The four triage questions, and the decision flow they make

blocks.md:
Triage (from the French *trier*, to sort) is borrowed from emergency medicine, where it means sorting patients by urgency when there are more of them than doctors. In a SOC it means a short, structured first look that ends in one of three outcomes: close it, keep investigating, or escalate now. The NCSC says triage depends on context: "Without a contextual grasp of the system, alerts will be difficult to triage."

Four questions, asked in order, carry most of the weight:

1. **What fired?** Read the rule, not just its name. What exactly does it match, and what does it *not* see?
2. **Is the data right?** Was the event parsed correctly, is the timestamp in the right zone, is the sensor healthy, is this a duplicate or a test?
3. **Is it expected?** Is there a change ticket, a known admin task, a scheduled scan, a penetration test, a user whose job explains it?
4. **What is the blast radius?** If this is real, what can the account, host or key reach, and is anything already happening?

Here is a synthetic alert. Before reading further, try the four questions on it yourself. Like every sample in this course it is invented, and its IP addresses come from ranges that [RFC 5737](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5737.txt) reserves for documentation.

blocks.md:
Walking it through:

- **What fired?** Someone granted `super_admin`, the highest role in the identity provider (IdP: the service that checks who you are and issues sign-in sessions, such as Okta or Microsoft Entra ID). The rule logs grants of the two top roles only; it would not see a smaller role that can still reset passwords.
- **Is the data right?** Find the raw event `evt-77f1c0` in the IdP's own log. Does it say the same actor, target and time? Rules sometimes mis-map fields.
- **Is it expected?** Look for an approved change ticket. Help desk staff granting super admin is unusual in most organisations; an approved, time-limited request from the identity team would be expected.
- **Blast radius?** A super admin can reset anyone's MFA (multi-factor authentication: a second proof such as a phone prompt or security key), add identity providers and change policies. If this is malicious, it is a whole-company problem, so this alert outranks its "medium" label.

blocks.title: The triage decision flow, applied to A-2041

nodes.label:
Rule matched wrongly:
false positive, tune

Data broken: fix the
source, flag the rule

Expected: benign true
positive, record why

scenes.caption: Start at the top: read what the rule matched. Here it matched a super_admin grant, a real event type the rule was built for. No sign the rule matched the wrong thing.
If the rule had matched something it should not (wrong field, bad pattern), stop: close as false positive, incorrect logic, and send the rule back for tuning.
Is the data right? The raw IdP event agrees with the alert: same actor, target, role, time. Had the log been malformed or duplicated, the fix is the data source, not the user.

Is it expected? Branch one: change ticket CHG-204 asks for exactly this grant, approved by the identity team lead, expiring tonight. That is a benign true positive: real, but expected. Record the ticket and close.
Branch two: no ticket, and the help desk account did it four minutes after an MFA reset for raj.patel. Not expected, so on to blast radius.
Super admin over the whole IdP: the radius is the entire company. Escalate now and say why. Lesson 7 shows the real attacks this pattern comes from.

blocks.md: "Expected" needs evidence: a ticket, a calendar entry, a confirmation through a channel the attacker does not control. "The user is an admin, admins do this" is a guess. Attackers who steal admin accounts do exactly what admins do.

Two habits make the four questions fast:

- **Read the raw event**, not just the alert summary. The summary is the rule author's interpretation; the raw event is the evidence.
- **Time-box the first look.** Triage should take minutes. If the questions cannot be answered quickly, that itself is the answer: move to investigation (and say what is still unknown) rather than leaving the alert half-read in the queue.

blocks.prompt: Alert: "PowerShell downloaded a file" on WEB-PROD-01 at 02:00 UTC. The deployment calendar shows a release at 02:00, run by the web team's pipeline account. The download URL is the company's own artifact server. Which question has the strongest answer, and what is your verdict?
blocks.reveal: Question 3, *is it expected?*, has a documented yes: a scheduled release by the pipeline account pulling from the company's artifact server. If the raw event confirms the account, URL and time match the release, this is a **benign true positive**: the rule correctly saw PowerShell downloading, and it was legitimate. Record the release ID in the note. If the account, URL or time did *not* match the release, the same alert would deserve a much closer look, because attackers like to hide inside release windows.

blocks.question: An alert says "login from new country" for a user, but the raw event shows the country field is empty and the SIEM's geolocation lookup defaulted to the first entry in its table. Which question caught this, and what is the right action?
options: Question 1; tune the rule to ignore that user
Question 3; ask the user whether they travelled
Question 4; escalate because geolocation failures can hide attacks
Question 2, the data is wrong; fix the enrichment or parser and note that the rule fired on bad data
blocks.explain: The data is wrong, so the user's behaviour has not been shown to be unusual at all. Microsoft Sentinel even has a separate closing reason for this, false positive due to incorrect data. The fix belongs to the pipeline, and the note tells the engineers what broke.

blocks.question: Why should the blast radius question sometimes raise an alert above the severity its rule assigned?
options: Because severity labels are always wrong
Because escalating more alerts improves metrics
Because the rule author set severity for the rule in general, while blast radius depends on this specific account, host or key and what it can reach
Because medium alerts are never investigated
blocks.explain: A rule's severity is a default written before anyone knew which account would trigger it. A super admin, a domain controller or a production cloud key has a far bigger blast radius than a test account, so the same rule can deserve very different urgency.

lessons.title: Verdicts, severity and priority: true, false and benign positives

blocks.md:
When an alert closes it gets a **verdict**. The words follow one pattern: *positive* means the rule fired, *true* or *false* says whether it was right to.

- **True positive (TP)**: the rule fired and the activity is malicious or a real policy violation.
- **False positive (FP)**: the rule fired but it should not have, because its logic matched the wrong thing or the data was wrong.
- **Benign true positive (BTP)**: the rule fired correctly on what it was built to see, but the activity was legitimate: an admin's planned change, a penetration test, a backup job.
- **False negative (FN)**: an attack with no alert. It never appears in the queue, which is why hunting exists.

Tools spell these differently. Microsoft Sentinel offers *True Positive: suspicious activity*, *Benign Positive: suspicious but expected*, *False Positive: incorrect alert logic*, *False Positive: incorrect data* and *Undetermined*. Microsoft Defender XDR calls the benign case *Informational, expected activity* and suggests it for security tests, red team activity and expected unusual behaviour.

The difference between FP and BTP matters because they need different fixes. A false positive means the **rule** is wrong and should be tuned. A benign true positive means the rule is right, and the fix (if any) is **context**: an exception for that job, a tag for that account, a change ticket the rule can check. Lumping both under "false positive" makes good rules look broken and leads teams to delete detections that were working.

The heatmap counts a synthetic month of closed alerts by rule and verdict. Read each column as one rule's track record.

blocks.title: One month of verdicts per rule (synthetic counts)

scenes.caption: Each column is a rule, each row a verdict. Totals: 60, 50, 5, 10 and 40 alerts. Precision, the share that were real, is the TP row divided by the column total.
Outbound to bad IP: 39 of 40 were false positives. That pattern (stale intel, shared CDN addresses, lesson 5) says fix the rule or its feed, not the analysts.
Impossible travel: 40 benign true positives, mostly VPN users. The rule sees what it should; it lacks context about the VPN. Precision 3 of 60, or 5 percent.
Shadow copies deleted: only 5 alerts, 3 real. Rare and usually real: an alert that should jump the queue every time it fires.

blocks.md: **A real case of alerts not acted on: Target, 2013.** Attackers used credentials stolen from an HVAC (heating, ventilation and air conditioning) contractor, Fazio Mechanical, to get into Target's network, then installed memory-scraping malware on point-of-sale terminals. A US Senate Commerce Committee staff report (2014), drawing on Bloomberg Businessweek reporting, says Target's FireEye malware detection system "triggered urgent alerts with each installation of the data exfiltration malware", and that Target's Symantec antivirus also flagged the same server around November 28. The security team "neither reacted to the alarms nor allowed the FireEye software to automatically delete the malware". Data flowed out for about two weeks; Target learned of the breach when the US Department of Justice notified it on December 12.

The report's explanation is the lesson for triage: the FireEye alert carried the generic name "malware.binary", and "it is possible that Target staff could have viewed this alert as a false positive if the system was frequently alarming". Two things went wrong at once. A noisy alert stream had trained people to dismiss alerts, and a rule with a vague name gave no reason to stop and look. Better triage would have asked question 4 (this is a payment network server) and noticed the same server flagged by a second, independent product. The NCSC makes the same point in general terms: real attacks often trigger multiple detections, so alerts that agree with each other deserve more weight.

Now **severity versus priority**:

- **Severity**: how bad it would be *if* the alert is a true positive. Set by the rule author, ahead of time.
- **Priority**: what to work on *now*. It combines severity with this alert's context: how critical the asset is, how often this rule is right, how far the attack seems to have got.

NIST SP 800-61r3 lists example "risk evaluation factors" for prioritising: asset criticality, functional impact, data impact, stage of observed activity, threat actor characterisation and recoverability. It also says the set "can range from simple to incredibly complex". The function below is a deliberately simple, illustrative way to fold three of those ideas (impact via the rule's severity, asset criticality and stage) plus the rule's track record into a number. It is not a standard; real SOCs tune their own.

blocks.code:
SEVERITY = {"low": 1, "medium": 2, "high": 3, "critical": 4}
ASSET = {"low": 1, "medium": 2, "high": 3}
LATE_STAGE = {"exfiltration", "impact"}   # harm may already be happening

def priority(a):
    """Illustrative only: one way to fold NIST's risk factors
    (asset criticality, impact, stage, confidence) into a number."""
    score = SEVERITY[a["severity"]] * ASSET[a["asset"]]
    score *= a["precision"]            # share of past alerts that were real
    if a["stage"] in LATE_STAGE:
        score += 6
    return round(score, 2)

# SYNTHETIC queue in arrival order
queue = [
    {"id": "A1", "rule": "Impossible travel", "severity": "high",
     "asset": "low", "precision": 0.05, "stage": "initial-access"},
    {"id": "A2", "rule": "AV quarantined file", "severity": "medium",
     "asset": "medium", "precision": 0.10, "stage": "execution"},
    {"id": "A3", "rule": "Shadow copies deleted", "severity": "high",
     "asset": "high", "precision": 0.60, "stage": "impact"},
    {"id": "A4", "rule": "New admin on IdP", "severity": "medium",
     "asset": "high", "precision": 0.40, "stage": "persistence"},
]
for a in sorted(queue, key=priority, reverse=True):
    print(a["id"], a["rule"], priority(a))
blocks.caption: priority.py: severity x asset criticality x the rule's historical precision, plus a bump for late-stage activity. Precisions match the heatmap.

A3 Shadow copies deleted 11.4
A4 New admin on IdP 2.4
A2 AV quarantined file 0.4
A1 Impossible travel 0.15
blocks.caption: Output. A1 arrived first and carries "high" severity, but on a low-value account with a 5 percent track record it goes last.

blocks.md: Using a rule's historical precision in priority has a trap: a rule that is usually wrong will sink to the bottom forever, including the one time it is right. Precision should make you fix the rule, not ignore it. Target's "malware.binary" alerts are the cautionary tale.

blocks.question: A rule detects `vssadmin delete shadows`. It fires because the backup product deletes old shadow copies every night at 01:00, exactly as configured. What is the verdict, and what is the fix?
options: False positive; delete the rule
True positive; escalate to incident response
Benign true positive; record the backup schedule and add a narrow, documented exception for that product's signed process at that time
Undetermined; leave it open
blocks.explain: The rule saw exactly what it was built to see, so it is not a false positive. The activity is legitimate, so it is not an attack. The fix is context: a narrow exception tied to the backup product, not deleting a rule that catches ransomware precursors.

blocks.question: Two alerts arrive at once. Alert X: severity critical, on a test VM that holds no data, from a rule that is right 2 percent of the time. Alert Y: severity medium, on the payroll database server, from a rule that is right 40 percent of the time. Which should normally be worked first, and why?
options: Y, because priority weighs severity against asset criticality and the rule's track record, and Y wins on both
X, because critical always beats medium
Whichever arrived first
Neither until both rules are tuned
blocks.explain: Severity is only one input. Y sits on a crown-jewel asset and comes from a rule that is right far more often. That is the point of separating severity (bad if true) from priority (what to do now).

lessons.title: Enrichment: asset, identity and intel context, and where it lies

blocks.md:
In Python for security you enriched an indicator by asking an outside API about it. Most of what an analyst needs, though, lives *inside* the organisation. **Enrichment** means attaching that context to an alert before or during triage, so the four questions can be answered in seconds:

- **Asset inventory**: what is this host, who owns it, how critical is it? Often kept in a CMDB (configuration management database: the register of IT assets and how they relate).
- **Identity context**: who is this user, which department, who is their manager, are they an admin, where do they normally sign in from?
- **Threat intelligence reputation**: has anyone reported this IP, domain or hash as malicious, and when?
- **Geolocation**: roughly where an IP address is registered or observed.
- **Past alerts**: has this host, user or indicator been in the queue before, and what was the verdict?

NIST SP 800-61r3 recommends exactly this: integrate threat intelligence "and other contextual information (e.g., asset inventories)" into analysis "to improve detection accuracy".

import csv, json
from datetime import date

def load(assets_csv, ids_json, intel_json):
    with open(assets_csv, newline="") as f:
        assets = {row["ip"]: row for row in csv.DictReader(f)}
    with open(ids_json) as f:
        ids = json.load(f)
    with open(intel_json) as f:
        intel = json.load(f)
    return assets, ids, intel

def enrich(alert, assets, ids, intel, today):
    out = dict(alert)              # never mutate the original
    asset = assets.get(alert["src_ip"])
    out["asset"] = asset or "UNKNOWN ASSET: ask why"
    person = ids.get(alert["user"])
    out["identity"] = person or "UNKNOWN USER: ask why"
    hit = intel.get(alert["dest_ip"])
    if hit:
        age = (today - date.fromisoformat(hit["last_seen"])).days
        out["intel"] = {**hit, "age_days": age,
                        "stale": age > 30}
    else:
        out["intel"] = "no record (not the same as clean)"
    tags = []
    if asset and asset["criticality"] == "high":
        tags.append("crown-jewel")
    if person and person["admin"]:
        tags.append("privileged-user")
    if hit and hit["verdict"] == "malicious" and age > 30:
        tags.append("stale-intel: re-check")
    out["tags"] = tags
    return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
    a, i, t = load("assets.csv", "identities.json", "intel.json")
    alert = {"id": "A-1009", "rule": "Outbound to known-bad IP",
             "src_ip": "10.10.1.12", "user": "raj.patel",
             "dest_ip": "203.0.113.50"}
    print(json.dumps(enrich(alert, a, i, t, date(2026, 11, 13)),
                     indent=1))

blocks.md:
Every enrichment source can mislead. The four classic traps:

- **Shared IP addresses.** Mobile carriers and many ISPs put thousands of customers behind one public IPv4 address (carrier-grade NAT). RFC 6269, the IETF's survey of address sharing, warns that "IP blocking for abuse/spam will cause collateral damage" and that traceability of abuse suffers. An IP's bad reputation may belong to a different customer.
- **CDN addresses.** A CDN (content delivery network: a provider whose edge servers serve many websites from shared addresses) puts unrelated sites on the same IPs. One malicious site on a CDN can paint an IP that also serves your payroll SaaS (software as a service: an application the vendor runs and you use over the web). That is the most likely story behind the 39 false positives in the previous lesson's "Outbound to bad IP" column.

- **Reputation lag.** Intel describes the past. Infrastructure is rented, abandoned and re-used, so last year's malicious IP may be a clean cloud host today, and today's attacker IP may not be in any feed yet. "No record" is not the same as clean.
- **Geolocation is approximate.** MaxMind, a major IP geolocation vendor, estimates country-level accuracy at 99.8 percent but city-level (within 50 km) at about 66 percent for US addresses, and notes that for a VPN user it locates the VPN server, not the person. Attackers know this: in the SolarWinds intrusion (a 2020 espionage campaign that lesson 7 tells in full), Mandiant (then FireEye) found the attackers "primarily used only IP addresses originating from the same country as the victim", via rented virtual private servers, so a country check saw nothing odd.

Enrichment answers "what is this thing?", not "is this bad?". Treat every enriched field as a claim with a source and an age, show unknowns explicitly, and never let a single reputation score close or escalate an alert by itself.

blocks.question: Enrichment says the source IP of a failed-login burst is "malicious (feed-A, last seen 2 years ago)" and geolocates to a mobile carrier. What is the soundest reading?
options: Confirmed attacker; block the IP everywhere
Weak evidence: the intel is old and carrier IPs are shared by many subscribers, so judge the alert on the login pattern itself
Definitely benign, because carrier IPs are always legitimate users
Ignore the alert, since enrichment disagrees with itself
blocks.explain: Both enrichment facts are weak: stale reputation, and an address that many unrelated customers share. Blocking it could cut off your own mobile users (collateral damage, in RFC 6269's words). The behaviour in the logs is better evidence than the label.

lessons.title: Suspicious logins: impossible travel and MFA push spam

blocks.md:
Many intrusions start with a login, not an exploit: Uber and every Snowflake case in this course began with valid credentials, and MGM's breach reportedly began with a help desk call that handed some over. The evidence lives in the IdP's **sign-in log**: one record per attempt, with user, time, source IP, device, app, whether MFA was asked for, and the result.

**Impossible travel** is the classic identity alert. Microsoft's documentation for Defender for Cloud Apps describes it as "two user activities ... originating from geographically distant locations within a time period shorter than the time it would have taken the user to travel from the first location to the second, indicating that a different user is using the same credentials." The check itself is simple arithmetic: distance between the two geolocated points, divided by the time between the sign-ins.

blocks.caption: The haversine formula: great-circle distance between two points with latitudes phi and longitudes lambda on a sphere of radius r (6371 km for Earth), then the implied speed v.

blocks.code:
from math import radians, sin, cos, asin, sqrt
from datetime import datetime

def km_between(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2):
    # haversine: great-circle distance on a sphere of radius 6371 km
    p1, p2 = radians(lat1), radians(lat2)
    dp, dl = p2 - p1, radians(lon2 - lon1)
    h = sin(dp / 2) ** 2 + cos(p1) * cos(p2) * sin(dl / 2) ** 2
    return 2 * 6371 * asin(sqrt(h))

def implied_speed(a, b):
    km = km_between(a["lat"], a["lon"], b["lat"], b["lon"])
    t1 = datetime.fromisoformat(a["time"])
    t2 = datetime.fromisoformat(b["time"])
    hours = abs((t2 - t1).total_seconds()) / 3600
    return km, hours, km / hours if hours else float("inf")

# SYNTHETIC sign-ins for one user (locations come from IP geolocation)
london = {"time": "2026-11-13T08:02:00+00:00", "lat": 51.507, "lon": -0.128}
singapore = {"time": "2026-11-13T08:49:00+00:00", "lat": 1.352, "lon": 103.820}
km, h, kmh = implied_speed(london, singapore)
print(f"{km:.0f} km in {h:.2f} h = {kmh:.0f} km/h")
MAX_KMH = 1000  # tunable threshold, set above airliner speeds
print("impossible travel" if kmh > MAX_KMH else "plausible")

blocks.md:
The arithmetic is never the hard part. The hard part is that *impossible travel* is often perfectly possible for a packet: a corporate VPN that exits in another country, a phone on mobile data while the laptop is on office Wi-Fi, a cloud proxy, a browser privacy relay. Microsoft's detection tries to ignore "obvious false positives" such as VPNs and locations other users in the organisation use regularly, and needs an initial learning period of seven days for each new user. Even so, expect many benign true positives (lesson 4's heatmap: 40 of 60).

Triage it with questions the formula cannot answer:

- Did *both* sign-ins pass MFA, and with which method?
- Is either IP a known VPN, proxy or cloud egress for the company?
- Same device and browser as usual, or new ones?
- What did each session do afterwards: read mail, create inbox rules, download files, change MFA settings?

**MFA push spam.** Push MFA sends an "Approve sign-in?" prompt to the user's phone. An attacker who already has the password can trigger prompt after prompt. MITRE ATT&CK (a public knowledge base of attacker behaviour, organised into tactics, the goal, and techniques, the method) files this as **T1621, Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation**, and notes that repeated attempts to bombard users with prompts can end with "the user finally accepting the authentication request in response to 'MFA fatigue'". CISA (the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) [calls it](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/fact-sheet-implement-number-matching-in-mfa-applications-508c.pdf) "push bombing".

**Uber, September 2022.** Uber's own update says an external contractor's password was likely bought on the dark web after malware infected the contractor's personal device. The attacker "repeatedly tried to log in"; each time the contractor got a two-factor approval request, which "initially blocked access. Eventually, however, the contractor accepted one". From there the attacker reached other employee accounts and elevated permissions in tools including G-Suite and Slack.

blocks.title: A push storm, the approval, and the SOC's response (synthetic times)

scenes.caption: 23:30. The attacker signs in with a bought password. The IdP sends a push to the real user's phone, which goes unanswered.
23:31 to 23:39. Six more attempts, six more pushes. The user denies some and ignores others. Each one is a line in the sign-in log.
23:41. Tired, or assuming it is an IT test, the user taps Approve. The attacker gets a session.
The pattern (many failures, then a success) is what the detection looks for. The alert reaches the SOC within a minute.
The analyst calls the user on the number in the HR record, not by replying in chat or email the attacker might control. The user says they did not sign in.
Contain: revoke all sessions, reset the password, review the MFA device list, then investigate what the session did in its minutes of access.

blocks.code:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

def push_storms(events, window_min=10, threshold=5):
    """events: dicts with time, user, result, sorted by time.
    Flags users with many denied or ignored pushes in a short
    window, and whether a push was then approved."""
    by_user = {}
    for e in events:
        by_user.setdefault(e["user"], []).append(e)
    findings = []
    for user, evs in by_user.items():
        bad = [e for e in evs if e["result"] in ("denied", "timeout")]
        for i, first in enumerate(bad):
            start = datetime.fromisoformat(first["time"])
            end = start + timedelta(minutes=window_min)
            burst = [e for e in bad[i:]
                     if datetime.fromisoformat(e["time"]) <= end]
            if len(burst) >= threshold:
                approved = [e for e in evs if e["result"] == "approved"
                            and datetime.fromisoformat(e["time"]) > start]
                findings.append({"user": user, "pushes": len(burst),
                                 "then_approved": bool(approved)})
                break
    return findings

# SYNTHETIC: 7 unanswered or denied pushes, then an approval at 23:41
log = [{"time": f"2026-11-12T23:{m:02d}:00", "user": "ana.silva",
        "result": r} for m, r in [(30, "timeout"), (31, "denied"),
        (33, "timeout"), (34, "denied"), (36, "timeout"),
        (37, "denied"), (39, "timeout"), (41, "approved")]]
print(push_storms(log))

blocks.code: [{'user': 'ana.silva', 'pushes': 7, 'then_approved': True}]
blocks.caption: Output: seven bad pushes in ten minutes, then an approval. That last field turns a nuisance into an urgent case.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** *Prevent*: CISA recommends phishing-resistant MFA (methods built on the Web Authentication standard, WebAuthn, such as security keys and passkeys), and number matching (the user types into the app a number shown on the sign-in screen) as an interim step, because it stops a blind tap from approving. *Detect*: bursts of MFA failures for one user, especially late at night (the CSRB, the US Cyber Safety Review Board, noted Lapsus$ prompts "sometimes ... occurred late at night"), and any success right after a burst. *Respond*, as Uber did: block or reset compromised accounts, rotate keys, require re-authentication, and add monitoring.

The CSRB's review of the group known as Lapsus$ found that, in a few cases, the attackers "impersonated help desk personnel over direct chat messages and encouraged employees to approve the MFA prompts". When you contact a user about an alert, use a channel the attacker cannot be sitting in, and teach users that the real SOC never asks them to approve a prompt.

blocks.question: Impossible travel fires: a sign-in from Paris, then from Toronto 40 minutes later. Both passed MFA by the same phone, the Toronto IP belongs to the company's VPN provider, and the user agent and device ID match the user's laptop. Best verdict?
options: True positive: credentials stolen
False positive: the haversine formula is wrong
Undetermined: escalate to incident response
Benign true positive: the travel is impossible for a person but explained by the VPN; record it and suggest adding the VPN egress to the rule's known locations
blocks.explain: The rule correctly measured an impossible speed between two IPs, so it is not a false positive. The context (company VPN, same device, MFA passed on the user's phone) explains it, so it is benign. The note should feed a context fix, not a rule deletion.

blocks.question: Which single field most changes the urgency of a push-storm alert?
options: Whether a push was approved after the storm
The number of pushes
The user's department
The phone's operating system
blocks.explain: Many denied pushes mean the attacker has the password but not the account yet: urgent, but contained (reset the password). An approval after a storm means the attacker may already hold a session, so revoke it now and find out what it did.

lessons.title: When the attacker calls the help desk: MFA resets and new devices

blocks.md:
MFA stops an attacker who only has a password. So attackers go after the *process* that gives people new MFA devices: the IT help desk. A caller says "I'm Raj, I got a new phone, I'm locked out", and a well-meaning technician resets the account's MFA. From the identity provider's point of view, everything that follows is legitimate.

CISA and the FBI's advisory AA23-320A on the group known as **Scattered Spider** describes the pattern. The group has "posed as employees to convince IT and/or helpdesk staff to provide sensitive information, reset the employee's password, and transfer the employee's MFA to a device they control", has also posed as IT staff to employees, used push bombing (T1621) and SIM swapping (convincing a mobile carrier to move a victim's phone number to the attacker's SIM card; SIM is the subscriber identity module), and in later intrusions encrypted VMware ESXi servers (ESXi, which AA23-320A expands as Elastic Sky X integrated, is VMware's hypervisor, the layer that runs many virtual machines).

**MGM Resorts, September 2023.** Slot machines and hotel room key cards stopped working at MGM casinos in Las Vegas. [Ars Technica](https://arstechnica.com/security/2023/09/a-phone-call-to-helpdesk-was-likely-all-it-took-to-hack-mgm/), republishing the Financial Times, reported that Scattered Spider was the likely culprit and that "a phone call to helpdesk was likely all it took". MGM did not respond to the reporters' request for comment, so treat the method as reported, not confirmed.

Ten days before MGM discovered its breach (August 31, 2023), Okta, the identity provider company, published what it had seen: several US customers reported callers convincing their IT service desk "to reset all Multi-factor Authentication (MFA) factors enrolled by highly privileged users". The attackers then signed in through anonymising proxies from "an IP and device not previously associated with the user account", gave more privileges to other accounts, and even added a second identity provider so they could impersonate other users.

Okta's post lists concrete System Log queries a SOC can alert on. Three matter most here:

- `eventType eq "user.mfa.factor.reset_all"`: all of a user's factors were reset.
- `eventType eq "user.session.start" and securityContext.isProxy eq "true"`: a sign-in through an anonymising proxy.
- `eventType eq "system.idp.lifecycle.create"`: someone created a new identity provider.

Each is weak alone; help desk resets happen every day. Together, in order, within minutes, on a privileged account, they tell a story. That is a job for **correlation**: joining records from different systems by user and time. ATT&CK files the attacker's step of enrolling their own device under T1098.005, Account Manipulation: Device Registration.

blocks.code:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

def ts(s):
    return datetime.fromisoformat(s)

def risky_resets(tickets, idp_events, admins, window=timedelta(hours=2)):
    """Join help desk tickets to identity-provider events: an MFA reset
    followed soon by a sign-in from a never-seen IP and device."""
    findings = []
    resets = [e for e in idp_events if e["type"] == "mfa.factor.reset_all"]
    for r in resets:
        user, t0 = r["user"], ts(r["time"])
        ticket = next((t for t in tickets if t["user"] == user
                       and abs(ts(t["time"]) - t0) < window), None)
        later = [e for e in idp_events if e["user"] == user
                 and e["type"] == "session.start"
                 and t0 < ts(e["time"]) <= t0 + window
                 and e["new_ip"] and e["new_device"]]
        if later:
            findings.append({
                "user": user, "admin": user in admins,
                "ticket": ticket["id"] if ticket else "NO TICKET",
                "caller_verified_by": ticket["verified_by"] if ticket else None,
                "first_new_signin": later[0]["time"]})
    return findings

# SYNTHETIC records
tickets = [{"id": "HD-5521", "user": "raj.patel", "time": "2026-11-13T14:02",
            "verified_by": "employee ID + date of birth"}]
idp = [{"type": "mfa.factor.reset_all", "user": "raj.patel",
        "time": "2026-11-13T14:06"},
       {"type": "session.start", "user": "raj.patel", "time": "2026-11-13T14:19",
        "new_ip": True, "new_device": True}]
print(risky_resets(tickets, idp, admins={"raj.patel"}))
blocks.caption: helpdesk.py: join help desk tickets with IdP events. A reset followed within two hours by a sign-in from a new IP and a new device is worth a human's attention, more so for an admin.

scenes.caption: 14:02. A caller claiming to be raj.patel asks the help desk to reset MFA. A ticket is opened, verified with employee ID and date of birth.
14:06. The technician resets all MFA factors. The IdP logs user.mfa.factor.reset_all. Routine, on its own.
14:19. A sign-in for raj.patel from an IP and device never seen before, through a proxy. The attacker enrols their own phone.
The correlation rule joins all three records by user and time window and raises one high-priority alert, because raj.patel is a super admin.
The analyst calls the real raj.patel on the number in the HR record: no, they called nobody. Revoke sessions and the new factor, freeze admin changes, escalate. Then check what the session did.
Had the SOC missed it, the next step in Okta's account of the attacks was admin actions: more privileges for other accounts, a new identity provider for impersonation.

blocks.md: **How SolarWinds was discovered: one routine MFA alert.** On November 10, 2020, according to Wired's reconstruction, Henna Parviz, an analyst at Mandiant (then part of FireEye), responded to "a routine security alert" of the kind raised whenever an employee enrolled a new phone in the company's MFA system. The new Samsung device had no phone number. Its VPN sign-ins came from an IP address in Florida, where the employee did not live, at the same time as sign-ins from the employee's old, still-enrolled iPhone. Kevin Mandia, the company's CEO, told [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2021/04/16/985439655/a-worst-nightmare-cyberattack-the-untold-story-of-the-solarwinds-hack) what happened next: the team called the employee, "and that phone call is when we realized, hey, this isn't our employee registering that second phone".

That thread led, over the following weeks, to a backdoor hidden in signed updates of SolarWinds Orion (IT monitoring software); Mandiant published its [analysis of the SUNBURST backdoor](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/evasive-attacker-leverages-solarwinds-supply-chain-compromises-with-sunburst-backdoor/) in December 2020. A supply chain attack against thousands of organisations surfaced because one analyst took a routine enrollment alert seriously and checked it against the user.

The help desk is part of your attack surface and part of your sensor network. Alert on MFA resets and new device enrollments for privileged users, correlate them with what happens next, and verify with the real person through a channel the caller cannot control. Okta also recommends stronger help desk identity checks, such as visual verification.

blocks.question: A help desk resets MFA for a finance clerk at 10:00 after a call. At 10:05 the clerk's account signs in from a new device through an anonymising proxy and creates a mail rule forwarding all mail with "invoice" to an outside address. What do you do first?
options: Close: the help desk ticket shows the reset was authorised
Email the clerk to ask whether they set up the rule
Revoke the sessions and the new factor, remove the forwarding rule, and verify with the clerk by phone on the HR-listed number
Wait for a second alert to confirm
blocks.explain: The ticket proves only that someone called. A new device through a proxy within minutes, followed by a forwarding rule aimed at invoices, is classic account takeover. Contain first, then verify out of band. Emailing the account the attacker may control is the wrong channel.

blocks.question: Why did the SolarWinds discovery start from a *routine* alert?
options: Because high-severity alerts were switched off
Because a careful analyst checked an MFA enrollment alert against what they knew about the user (location, existing devices, simultaneous sessions) and found contradictions
Because the backdoor itself raised the alert
Because the employee reported the phone
blocks.explain: Per Wired and NPR, the alert only said a new phone was enrolled. The analyst noticed it had no phone number, signed in from a state the employee did not live in, and was active at the same time as the employee's real phone, then called the employee. Context, not severity, made it matter.

lessons.title: Malware on an endpoint: reading a process tree

blocks.md:
Endpoint alerts come from EDR (endpoint detection and response: an agent on each computer that records process, file and network activity, raises alerts and can act, for example by isolating the machine from the network) or from Sysmon (System Monitor, Microsoft's free Sysinternals tool you met in the Windows course). The single most useful view of an endpoint alert is the **process tree**: which program started which, in order.

Every process has a parent, the process that created it. A normal tree for an office worker looks like `explorer.exe` (the Windows desktop shell) starting Word, Chrome or Teams. What makes analysts sit up is a parent and child that should never be related: Word starting a command shell, a PDF reader starting PowerShell, a web server process starting `whoami`.

Sysmon's Event ID 1 (process creation) records each new process with its parent. The documentation explains the key design choice: each event includes a **process GUID** (globally unique identifier) "to allow for correlation of events even when Windows reuses process IDs". A PID (process ID) is just a number Windows hands out and later recycles; the GUID is unique for that process. Build trees on GUIDs, never on PIDs. Sysmon timestamps are in UTC.

Here are three of the seven synthetic events from one Finance laptop. Event ID 5 records a process ending.
