scenes.caption: explorer.exe is the user's desktop shell. Everything the user launches by double-clicking hangs under it. Nothing unusual yet.
09:15:40. The user opens invoice_8812.docm from Downloads in Word. A .docm is a macro-enabled document. Opening a file is normal; the file type from an outside sender is worth noting.
09:15:52. Word starts cmd.exe. Office applications almost never need a shell. ATT&CK T1204.002, User Execution: Malicious File, is the likely start of the story.
09:15:53. cmd.exe starts PowerShell with -EncodedCommand: the script is base64-encoded so it is not readable in the command line. T1059.001, PowerShell.

09:16:20. PowerShell starts rundll32.exe on a DLL in the user's Temp folder. Rundll32 is a signed Windows binary, which is why attackers use it to run their code (T1218.011). Next pivot: its network connections.
09:20:11. notepad.exe with PID 7312. Linking by PID would wrongly hang it under Word, or confuse it with cmd.exe. Linking by GUID puts it under explorer.exe, where it belongs.

blocks.md:
What to check on each suspicious node, in roughly this order:

- **Path**: is the binary where it should be? `rundll32.exe` belongs in System32; the DLL it loads from a user's Temp folder does not belong anywhere trusted.
- **Command line**: encoded commands, download URLs, unusual flags.
- **Signer and hash**: is the file signed by its real publisher, and what do your intel sources say about the hash?
- **User and integrity**: which account, and was it elevated?
- **Children and side effects**: network connections from that process (Sysmon Event ID 3 links each connection to its ProcessGuid), files it wrote (Event ID 11), registry changes.

The Windows course covered how persistence and Event IDs look; here the question is narrower: *is this tree explainable by normal work?*

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: block macros in files from the internet, restrict which apps may start script interpreters, keep PowerShell logging on. *Detect*: rules on Office parent with shell child, encoded PowerShell, rundll32 loading from user-writable folders. *Respond*: this tree is a true positive until proven otherwise. Isolate the host through the EDR (Microsoft's documentation for its EDR, for example, says [isolation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/respond-machine-alerts) disconnects the device from the network while keeping its connection to the security service, so you can still investigate), do not wipe it before incident response has collected evidence, and pivot: the file name and hash to the mail system (who else received it?), the destination IP to proxy logs (who else connected?), the user to sign-in logs (lesson 12 builds the full timeline from exactly these pivots).

A process tree shows execution, not intent. Developer tools, installers and IT scripts produce strange trees every day. The tree tells you where to look; the evidence on each node (path, signer, command line, network) decides the verdict.

blocks.question: Your tree-building script links children to parents by ParentProcessId. Which bug will it produce?
options: None; PIDs are unique for the life of the machine
It will run too slowly
It will skip all processes started by SYSTEM
A process that started after its true parent exited can be attached to an unrelated earlier process that had the same PID, producing a false lineage
blocks.explain: Windows recycles PIDs, which is why Sysmon adds ProcessGuid. In the example, notepad.exe reused cmd.exe's PID 7312. Linking by PID can fabricate a malicious-looking tree, or hide a real one.

blocks.question: Four parent and child pairs appear in today's EDR data. Which deserves the fastest look?
options: explorer.exe starting WINWORD.EXE
explorer.exe starting chrome.exe
explorer.exe starting Teams.exe
WINWORD.EXE starting powershell.exe -EncodedCommand
blocks.explain: The first three are a user launching ordinary applications from the desktop. A word processor launching an encoded PowerShell command is a classic sign of a malicious document.

lessons.title: Phishing reports and unusual data egress

blocks.md:
A reported phish has its own analyst workflow (acknowledge, triage the headers, sandbox the links and attachments, scope, contain, close the loop), taught in full in the phishing and email security course. Inside a SOC, the part that connects a phish to everything else is **scoping by pivoting**: the same sender, subject, URL or attachment hash, searched across *all* mailboxes, then the URL across proxy logs and the attachment name or hash across EDR. That is how the `invoice_8812.docm` in the previous lesson's process tree would be tied back to the message that delivered it, and to every other person who received it.

This lesson's main subject is the other end of an intrusion: data leaving. **Egress** means outbound traffic; **exfiltration** is egress the owner did not want. ATT&CK lists many ways, among them T1048, Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (FTP or DNS instead of the attacker's command channel), and T1567.002, Exfiltration to Cloud Storage, which can "provide a significant amount of cover" when hosts already talk to that service.

**Target again.** The Senate report describes the end of the 2013 kill chain: the malware sent stolen card data to an external FTP (file transfer protocol) server via another compromised Target server, starting December 2, "in plain text via FTP", over about two weeks, with at least one destination in Russia. The report suggests allow-listing approved FTP destinations, and notes that while analysing a busy network's traffic "may be like searching for a needle in a haystack", an upload to such a server "presumably would have been flagged as suspicious if discovered". It also says the FireEye product had decoded the destination of the servers holding the stolen data.

The practical detection is simple to state: compare each host's outbound volume with *its own* history, not with the fleet. A build server uploading 9 GB a day is normal; a file server that usually sends 120 MB suddenly sending 6 GB is not.

blocks.caption: egress.py: flag hosts whose upload volume today is at least 10 times their own 7-day median, ignoring small absolute volumes.
Output: only the file server is flagged, at 52.5 times its usual daily volume.

blocks.title: The same numbers, three ways (synthetic MB uploaded)

scenes.caption: Today's raw upload volume. BUILD-07 towers over everything, so a dashboard ranked by bytes would point you at the build server, which does this every day.
Each host's own baseline: the median of the last 7 days. The median ignores a single odd day, which a mean would not.
Today divided by baseline: 1.15, 1.08 and 52.5. Relative to its own normal, only the file server is strange. Same data, very different priority.

blocks.md:
Triage an egress alert with the four questions, made specific:

- **What fired?** A volume threshold, a new destination, a protocol the host never uses (FTP from a file server), or a known-bad destination?
- **Is the data right?** Flow records and proxy logs count bytes differently; check that the volume is real and not a counter reset or a duplicated log feed.
- **Is it expected?** Backups, replication to a disaster-recovery site, software updates and large legitimate uploads all produce spikes. Look for a change ticket or a scheduled job.
- **Blast radius?** Which **process** sent the data (EDR or Sysmon Event ID 3 ties connections to processes), to whom (who owns the destination IP or domain, and is it a service the company uses?), at what time of day, and what did that host read just before (file access logs)?

Volume alone is a weak signal; volume against the host's own baseline, plus the sending process and the destination's owner, is a strong one. Exfiltration to a popular cloud storage service will look normal by destination, so the process and the account doing the upload matter most.

blocks.question: A laptop's daily upload is normally about 50 MB. Today it sent 4 GB to a well-known cloud storage provider, and the company uses that provider. Which next step best separates exfiltration from normal work?
options: Close it: the provider is sanctioned
Block the provider for the whole company
Find which process and which account did the upload, and whether the destination account belongs to the company's tenant or someone else's
Geolocate the provider's IP address
blocks.explain: A sanctioned provider gives cover (T1567.002). The distinguishing facts are the process (the sync client or something odd?) and the destination tenant or account. Geolocation of a cloud provider's IP tells you where their data centre is, nothing more.

lessons.title: Cloud key misuse, and what Snowflake customers could see in 2024

blocks.md: In the cloud, a stolen **access key** (a long secret string that lets a program call the provider's API as a particular identity) is as good as a stolen password with no MFA in front of it. AWS (Amazon Web Services) makes the first triage step easy: the access key ID itself says what kind of credential it is. AWS's GuardDuty documentation explains that keys beginning **AKIA** are "a long term customer-managed credential associated with an IAM user or AWS account root user", while keys beginning **ASIA** are "a short term temporary credential generated by AWS Security Token Service". (IAM is Identity and Access Management, AWS's permission system; STS, the Security Token Service, issues temporary credentials, for example to a server or a role.) A leaked AKIA key works until someone deactivates it; an ASIA key expires on its own, but can still do a lot of damage first.

The evidence is in **CloudTrail**, AWS's log of API calls. One trap to know before an incident: CloudTrail's documentation says "By default, trails and event data stores do not log data events", which include reads of individual objects (files) in S3, Amazon Simple Storage Service. If nobody turned them on, you may see that a key listed buckets but not which files it read.

**GuardDuty** is AWS's managed threat detection service. One of its findings maps directly onto key theft: `UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS`, default severity High. It fires when temporary credentials created for an EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) instance, a virtual server, are used "from an external IP address", meaning the credentials may have been copied off the server.

The same page lists the classic benign true positive: networks routed so that traffic leaves through an on-premises gateway rather than AWS's internet gateway (for example over a VPN connection) produce this finding legitimately. The fix there is a narrow suppression rule for that finding type and that gateway's IP range. It also warns that if activity from one remote host continues, GuardDuty's machine-learning model will "identify this as an expected behavior" and stop generating the finding for that host. A slow analyst can let a real intruder become the baseline.

AWS's remediation guidance for a possibly compromised credential reads like a triage checklist: identify the IAM entity and the API call in the finding; review the entity's permissions; then "contact the user of the credentials" and confirm whether they made that call, at that time, from that IP. If you can confirm it, it is legitimate; "If you can't confirm", treat it as a possible compromise of the key, the user's sign-in credentials, or the whole account.

The script below runs the first part of that review over a simplified CloudTrail extract: what kind of key, any calls from unfamiliar networks, any discovery calls, any bulk reads.

blocks.caption: cloudkey.py: review one access key's recent CloudTrail activity (field names follow CloudTrail; records simplified and synthetic).

blocks.code: ('long-term (IAM user)', ["calls from unfamiliar IPs: ['203.0.113.77']", "discovery calls: ['GetCallerIdentity', 'ListBuckets']", '2400 object reads: possible bulk collection'])
blocks.caption: Output: a long-term key, a new source IP, the standard "who am I and what is here" calls, then 2,400 reads. The reads are only visible because S3 data events were enabled.

blocks.md:
**Snowflake, 2024: when the vendor was not breached but its customers were.** Snowflake is a cloud data warehouse. In June 2024 Mandiant reported a campaign by a group it tracks as UNC5537 (UNC is Mandiant's prefix for an uncategorized cluster of activity not yet tied to a named group) against Snowflake customer accounts. Every incident it responded to traced back to stolen customer credentials, mostly from **infostealer** malware (malware that harvests saved passwords from a computer), some stolen as early as November 2020. Three things made it work: the accounts had no MFA, the stolen credentials were still valid (some unrotated for years), and there were no network allow lists limiting where logins could come from. Mandiant and Snowflake notified about 165 potentially exposed organisations.

The detection story is humbling for SOCs: Mandiant first learned of it through threat intelligence about database records that had come from a victim's Snowflake instance, then notified the victim. The data had already left before most victims saw anything.

blocks.title: What a Snowflake customer's logs could show (from Mandiant's report)

scenes.caption: The attacker logs in with a username and password harvested by infostealer malware. No MFA, no network allow list. Mandiant saw mostly VPN exit addresses (Mullvad, Private Internet Access) as sources.
Reconnaissance: listing tables. Mandiant saw an attacker-named utility it tracks as FROSTBITE, and the database client DBeaver Ultimate, both visible in the login's client application field.
Staging: create a temporary stage (a storage area for data files), copy whole tables into it compressed with GZIP, then GET the files to the attacker's machine.
The first outside sign: data offered on criminal forums, picked up by threat intelligence. In April 2024 Mandiant traced records to a victim's instance and notified it.
The customer's SOC hunts its own login and query history: unfamiliar client application IDs, VPN source IPs, temporary stages, COPY INTO and GET from a user who never did that before.
Response: rotate credentials, enforce MFA, add network allow lists, and scope what each session read. Snowflake published detection and hardening guidance on May 30, 2024.

blocks.md: Cloud and SaaS triage starts with three questions: what kind of credential is this, where is it being used from compared with normal, and what did it touch. The third question can only be answered if the right logs (S3 data events, the warehouse's query history) were switched on and kept long enough before the incident.

blocks.question: GuardDuty raises InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS for a web server's role credentials. The source IP is the company's own on-premises VPN gateway, and the web team confirms the server routes outbound traffic through it. What is the right outcome?
options: Benign true positive: document it and add a suppression rule scoped to that finding type and the gateway's IP range
True positive: rotate everything and escalate
False positive: disable GuardDuty
Ignore it; GuardDuty will learn the behaviour anyway
blocks.explain: This is the benign case AWS describes, and AWS recommends exactly a two-criteria suppression rule. Letting the model learn it silently is worse: you lose the record of why, and the same learning would hide a real attacker on another host.

blocks.question: Mandiant's Snowflake investigation found that most stolen credentials had been exposed by infostealers long before use, some since 2020. Which control would have made those old credentials useless regardless of when they leaked?
options: Longer log retention
Requiring MFA (and network allow lists) on the accounts
A larger SOC team
Geolocation-based alerting
blocks.explain: Mandiant names missing MFA, unrotated credentials and missing network allow lists as the three factors. MFA and allow lists block a leaked password outright; logging and staffing only help you notice afterwards.

lessons.title: Ransomware precursors, and deciding fast: Colonial Pipeline

blocks.md:
Ransomware (malware that encrypts data and demands payment for the key) is usually the *last* step of an intrusion, after the attackers have spent days or weeks inside. Some of the last steps before encryption are loud enough to catch:

- **Recovery tampering**, ATT&CK T1490, Inhibit System Recovery. Attackers delete the copies that would let you undo the damage. ATT&CK lists the native Windows tools used, such as `vssadmin.exe` and `wmic` deleting **volume shadow copies** (Windows' built-in point-in-time snapshots of a disk), `wbadmin.exe` deleting the backup catalog, and `bcdedit.exe` turning off automatic recovery.
- **Mass file changes**, the visible side of T1486, Data Encrypted for Impact: one process renaming or rewriting hundreds of files a minute.
- Earlier signs worth a look on the same host: new remote access tools, credential dumping, security tools being stopped.

blocks.caption: ransom.py: two precursor checks over EDR or Sysmon events: recovery-tampering command lines, and file changes per minute per host. The command string is what defenders see in process logs.

blocks.code:
(5, 'FILE-SRV-02', 'recovery tampering: vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet')
(6, 'FILE-SRV-02', '1800 file changes/min')
(7, 'FILE-SRV-02', '1800 file changes/min')
(8, 'FILE-SRV-02', '1800 file changes/min')
blocks.caption: Output: the shadow copy deletion comes one minute before the storm of file changes.

blocks.title: File changes per minute on FILE-SRV-02 (synthetic)

scenes.caption: 09:00 to 09:04: normal churn, about 30 file modifications a minute from people saving documents.
09:05: no file changes, but a process runs vssadmin to delete every shadow copy. One alert, high severity, rare and usually real (lesson 4's heatmap).
09:06 to 09:08: 1,800 renames a minute. Encryption is under way. Every minute here is thousands of files.
09:09: the host is isolated and the storm stops. About 5,400 files were hit in three minutes.
Had the 09:05 alert been acted on within a minute, the storm would never have shown. Precursor alerts are worth an immediate, pre-approved response.

blocks.md: **Colonial Pipeline, May 2021.** Colonial runs the largest refined-products pipeline by volume in the US, more than 5,500 miles from Gulf Coast refineries to New York Harbor. Its CEO, Joseph Blount, gave the US Senate a minute-by-minute account. Just before 5:00 AM Eastern Daylight Time on Friday, May 7, "one of our employees identified the ransom note on a system in the IT network". The employee notified the Operations Supervisor at the Control Center, who put in a stop work order to halt the whole pipeline, to make sure the malware "did not spread to the Operational Technology (OT) network, which controls our pipeline operations, if it had not already." Shutdown began around 5:55 AM; by 6:10 all 5,500 miles were confirmed shut down, about fifteen minutes of work.

blocks.title: Colonial Pipeline, morning of May 7, 2021 (minutes after 04:50 EDT)

scenes.caption: Just before 05:00: an employee finds a ransom note on a system in the IT network. The exact minute is not public; the block is placed approximately.
"Shortly after", per the testimony: the Operations Supervisor issues a stop work order. Everyone at Colonial has stop work authority. Timing approximate.
About 05:55: employees begin shutting the pipeline down. Nobody yet knows where the attack started or how far it reached.
06:10: all 5,500 miles confirmed shut down, roughly fifteen minutes after the start. The same morning Colonial reached out to the FBI and set up a call with the FBI and CISA.

blocks.md:
Blount explained the reasoning: "When we learned of the attack, we did not know the point of origination of the attack nor the scope of it, so bringing the entire system down was the surest way ... to contain any potential damage." Colonial began returning all pipelines to service only on the evening of Wednesday, May 12, and the shutdown led to panic buying and shortages on the East Coast. The company later said the attacker had used "a legacy virtual private network (VPN) profile that was not intended to be in use"; Blount named the attackers as the cyber-criminal group DarkSide.

For an analyst, the lesson is not "shut everything down". It is that the decision to contain under uncertainty belongs to people with **pre-agreed authority**, and that the analyst's job is to get the facts to them in minutes, not to wait until the scope is clear. The scope is never clear at 5 AM.

Do not "watch it to learn more" once you see encryption or recovery tampering. Every minute of observation costs files. Escalate immediately with what you know, isolate if your playbook allows it, and let incident response decide about wider containment.

blocks.question: At 02:14 a shadow-copy deletion alert fires on a file server. No other alerts yet. The on-call IR lead is asleep. What is the best first move?
options: Wait until the morning shift and investigate then
Restore the shadow copies
Email the server owner and wait for a reply
Page the IR lead now, isolate the host if the playbook pre-authorises it, and start collecting the process tree and the account that ran the command
blocks.explain: Recovery tampering is a late-stage precursor, and encryption may be minutes away. Paging at 02:14 is exactly what on-call exists for. Pre-authorised isolation buys time; evidence about the process and account tells IR how far the intrusion has spread.

blocks.question: Colonial shut down the whole pipeline although the ransomware was found on the IT network, not on the systems controlling the pipeline. According to the CEO's testimony, why?
options: Because they did not know where the attack started or how far it had spread, and stopping the pipeline was the surest way to keep it from reaching the OT network
Because the OT network had already been encrypted
Because the ransom note demanded it
Because regulators ordered the shutdown
blocks.explain: The testimony says the stop work order aimed to keep the malware from spreading to the OT network "if it had not already", because the origin and scope were unknown. It is a textbook decision under uncertainty, made by people with authority to make it.

lessons.title: Pivoting, building a timeline, and mapping it to ATT&CK

blocks.md:
One alert is a single point. An investigation turns it into a story by **pivoting**: taking one indicator from the alert (a host, a user, a file hash, an IP, a domain) and searching *other* data sources for it, which surfaces new indicators to pivot on in turn. Each pivot either widens the story ("three other mailboxes got the same file") or bounds it ("no other host talked to that IP"); both results go in the notes.

Mandiant's SUNBURST write-up gives two pivots worth copying. The attackers used several IP addresses per hosting provider, so "once a malicious login from an unusual ASN is identified, looking at all logins from that ASN can help detect additional malicious activity" (an ASN, autonomous system number, identifies the network operator an IP address belongs to). And because the attackers moved between systems with many different accounts, Mandiant suggested looking for "any single system authenticating to multiple systems with multiple accounts, a relatively uncommon occurrence during normal business operations".

As you pivot, build a **timeline**: every relevant event, one line each, in time order, with its source. Two rules keep it honest:

- **One clock.** Convert everything to UTC. Sources disagree: Sysmon's documentation says its timestamps are UTC, a mail server may log with an offset, a proxy may log seconds since 1970 (Unix epoch time), and some appliance logs local time with no offset at all, which you must look up.
- **Facts separate from inferences.** "09:16:35 FIN-LT-042 connected to 203.0.113.50:443 [proxy]" is a fact. "This was command and control" is an inference, and gets labelled as one.

The script below merges four synthetic sources in four time formats.

blocks.code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta

def to_utc(raw, fmt):
    """Turn each source's timestamp format into aware UTC."""
    if fmt == "epoch":                    # seconds since 1970 UTC
        return datetime.fromtimestamp(int(raw), tz=timezone.utc)
    if fmt == "iso":                      # carries its own offset
        return datetime.fromisoformat(raw).astimezone(timezone.utc)
    if fmt == "sysmon":                   # UtcTime field is UTC
        dt = datetime.strptime(raw, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%f")
        return dt.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
    if fmt == "cet":                      # no offset in the data
        cet = timezone(timedelta(hours=1))
        dt = datetime.fromisoformat(raw).replace(tzinfo=cet)
        return dt.astimezone(timezone.utc)
    raise ValueError(f"unknown time format {fmt}")

def build(sources):
    rows = [(to_utc(t, fmt), name, what)
            for name, fmt, events in sources
            for t, what in events]
    return sorted(rows)

# SYNTHETIC events from four sources in four time formats
sources = [
  ("mail", "iso", [("2026-11-13T10:12:30+01:00",
                    "invoice_8812.docm delivered to ana.silva")]),
  ("edr", "sysmon", [("2026-11-13 09:15:40.220", "WINWORD opens the .docm"),
                     ("2026-11-13 09:16:20.477", "rundll32 runs Temp upd.dll")]),
  ("proxy", "epoch", [("1794561395", "FIN-LT-042 to 203.0.113.50:443")]),
  ("idp", "cet", [("2026-11-13T10:41:00", "ana.silva sign-in, new device")]),
]
for t, src, what in build(sources):
    print(t.strftime("%H:%M:%S"), f"{src:<6}", what)
blocks.caption: timeline.py: normalise each source's timestamps to UTC, then sort. Note the IdP source: its log has no offset, so the analyst must know it is CET (UTC+01:00) and say so.

blocks.code:
09:12:30 mail   invoice_8812.docm delivered to ana.silva
09:15:40 edr    WINWORD opens the .docm
09:16:20 edr    rundll32 runs Temp upd.dll
09:16:35 proxy  FIN-LT-042 to 203.0.113.50:443
09:41:00 idp    ana.silva sign-in, new device
blocks.caption: Output, all UTC. Read raw, the mail log said 10:12 and the IdP 10:41: an hour off, which would have put delivery after the infection.

scenes.caption: Start: the EDR alert. rundll32 ran a DLL from Temp at 09:16:20. One block, no story yet.
Pivot 1, host to process tree: Word opened a .docm at 09:15:40; cmd.exe and an encoded PowerShell started 12 and 13 seconds later. The alert now has a cause.
Pivot 2, file name to mail logs: the .docm arrived at 09:12:30, three minutes before it was opened. The same message reached three more mailboxes (unopened).
Pivot 3, host to proxy logs: 15 seconds after rundll32 started, the laptop connected to 203.0.113.50:443. No other host contacted that IP in seven days, which bounds the scope.
Pivot 4, user to identity logs: 25 minutes later, a sign-in as ana.silva from a device never seen before. This turns a malware case into an account compromise. Escalate.
Map each fact to ATT&CK. The last two are inferences (C2 over HTTPS, use of stolen credentials) until IR confirms them, and the note must say so.

blocks.md:
**Mapping to ATT&CK.** MITRE's design paper for ATT&CK explains its two main levels: tactics "represent the 'why'" of a technique (the attacker's goal, such as Initial Access or Execution), and techniques "represent 'how' an adversary achieves a tactical objective". Procedures are the specific way a particular group did it. Mapping the timeline above gives:

- T1566.001 Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment (Initial Access)
- T1204.002 User Execution: Malicious File, and T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell (Execution)
- T1218.011 System Binary Proxy Execution: Rundll32
- T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (Command and Control), inferred
- T1078 Valid Accounts, inferred

Why bother? A shared vocabulary lets IR and detection teams read your case instantly, the mapping shows how far the attack got, and gaps suggest where to look next. ATT&CK is versioned and sometimes renames or moves things; the current site, for example, lists Rundll32 under a tactic named Stealth. Record the version you mapped against.
Do not force-fit. If you cannot say which technique an event shows, write the plain fact and leave the ID out. A wrong mapping in a case note propagates into reports and detection gap analyses.

blocks.question: A firewall logs in local time without an offset (the appliance is set to UTC-05:00), and your EDR logs in UTC. A firewall line says 04:10 and an EDR line says 09:05. In UTC, which happened first?
options: The firewall event, at 04:10 UTC
They happened at the same moment
The EDR event: the firewall's 04:10 is 09:10 UTC, five minutes after the EDR's 09:05
It cannot be determined from timestamps
blocks.explain: Local 04:10 at UTC-05:00 is 09:10 UTC, five minutes after the EDR event. Ordering raw strings from mixed zones would have put the firewall event five hours earlier.

blocks.question: You pivot from a malicious IP to proxy logs and find no other host contacted it in the last 7 days. What should the case note say?
options: Nothing, since the search found nothing
That the scope is bounded: the exact query, the time range and that no other host connected, so others can trust (or extend) the check
That the IP is safe
That the proxy logs must be broken
blocks.explain: Negative results are findings. Recording the exact query and range lets IR rely on it, or rerun it over a longer window. It says nothing about the IP being safe.

lessons.title: When to escalate, and case notes someone else can act on

blocks.md:
**Escalation** hands a case to people with more time, skill or authority, usually incident response. NIST SP 800-61r3 frames it as a decision against criteria written in advance: "Incidents are declared when adverse events meet the defined incident criteria", applying those criteria "to known and assumed characteristics of analyzed activity" and considering known false positives. *Assumed* matters: you are allowed to escalate on what the evidence suggests, before it is proven.

Every SOC writes its own criteria. A typical set (illustrative) escalates when any of these holds:

- Confirmed or likely malicious activity on a privileged account or a critical asset.
- Late-stage signs: data leaving, recovery tampering, encryption.
- More than one host or account involved, or signs of movement between them.
- Possible personal or regulated data exposure (legal and privacy teams must hear early).
- A time box expires on a high-impact alert you still cannot explain.

Two failure modes sit on either side. **Escalating too late** is the costly one: Target's alerts, Colonial's minutes. **Escalating everything** is the slow one: incident responders drown, and real incidents wait behind noise. The cure for both is the same: a clear criteria list, permission to escalate on reasonable suspicion, and a case note good enough that the receiver can act without calling you back.

NIST lists what to track for each incident: "an incident summary, indicators of compromise related to the incident, the status and expected time frame for each assigned action, and next steps to be taken", and suggests designating an incident lead. The NCSC suggests designing alerts around the "5W1H" questions (who, what, when, where, why, how); case notes benefit from the same discipline. Here is a template built on both.

blocks.code:
CASE <id>  |  status: <open / escalated / closed>  |  TLP:<label>
SUMMARY (bottom line first, 2-3 sentences)
  What happened, to whom, how sure you are, what you need now.
VERDICT AND CONFIDENCE
  <true positive / benign true positive / false positive / undetermined>
  confidence <low / medium / high> because <evidence>
SCOPE
  Hosts: ...  Accounts: ...  Data possibly touched: ...
  Checked and clean: ...  (say what you looked at and found nothing)
TIMELINE (UTC, one line per fact, source in brackets)
  09:12:30 [mail] ...
EVIDENCE
  Queries run (exact text), event IDs, hashes, screenshots location
ACTIONS TAKEN (who, when, reversible?)
  ...
OPEN QUESTIONS
  ...
NEXT STEPS AND OWNERS (with times)
  ...
blocks.caption: case-note template. BLUF (bottom line up front) summary, explicit confidence, scope including what was checked and found clean, UTC timeline, exact evidence, reversible actions, owners and times.

blocks.code:
CASE C-312  |  status: escalated to IR (INC-0077)  |  TLP:AMBER+STRICT
SUMMARY
  ana.silva opened invoice_8812.docm at 09:15 UTC; it ran encoded
  PowerShell and a DLL from Temp on FIN-LT-042, which contacted
  203.0.113.50. At 09:41 an unknown device signed in as ana.silva.
  High confidence of compromise. Need IR to own scope of the account.
VERDICT  true positive, high: process tree + proxy + IdP agree
SCOPE
  Hosts: FIN-LT-042 (isolated 09:52). Accounts: ana.silva.
  Same message in 3 more mailboxes; none opened it (mail trace, 09:58).
  Checked and clean: no other host contacted 203.0.113.50 (proxy, 7 days).
TIMELINE  see attached; all times UTC
ACTIONS  09:52 host isolated via EDR (reversible); 09:55 sessions
  revoked and password reset for ana.silva; 09:58 message purged.
OPEN  What did the 09:41 session access? Was upd.dll seen elsewhere?
NEXT  IR lead (on-call) owns from 10:05; SOC watches for the hash
  and IP fleet-wide; user informed by phone 10:02.
blocks.caption: The same template filled in for the lesson 12 investigation (synthetic). Someone who has never seen the case can act on it.

blocks.title: Who reads your case note, and what each needs from it

scenes.caption: One note, many readers, most of whom were not there. Write it for them, not for yourself.
The incident lead reads the summary, verdict and scope first: is this an incident, how big, what is already contained?
The next shift reads open questions and next steps with owners and times, the same things a handover needs.
The system owner reads actions taken and whether they are reversible: their laptop is isolated, their account was reset.
The detection team reads the evidence and verdict to tune or add rules. Quality review, weeks later, reads why it was closed or escalated.

blocks.md: Write times in UTC with the date, paste exact queries rather than describing them, and separate "checked and clean" from "not checked". The most useful sentence in many notes is the one that says what you did not look at.

blocks.prompt: You have triaged a suspicious sign-in for 40 minutes. You are fairly sure it is an attacker, but you have not found what the session did. Your time box was 30 minutes. Escalate now, or keep digging until you know the impact?
blocks.reveal: Escalate now, with a note that says exactly that: likely compromise, confidence medium to high and why, actions already taken (sessions revoked?), and the open question "what did the session access". NIST's criteria explicitly allow assumed characteristics. Incident response can widen the search with more access and people. Waiting for certainty is how attackers get hours they should not have.

blocks.question: Which case-note summary lets an incident lead act fastest?
options: "Weird stuff on a laptop, see the logs"
"Malware alert. Ran some queries. Looks bad."
"FIN-LT-042 ran a malicious macro at 09:15 UTC; an unknown device signed in as the user at 09:41. Host isolated, sessions revoked. Need IR to scope the account's access."
A copy of the full raw logs with no summary
blocks.explain: It states what happened, when, to what, how sure, what is already done and what is needed. The others force the reader to redo the triage.

blocks.question: Why should a case note list what was checked and found clean?
options: To make the note longer
Because auditors only read negative results
It should not; only findings belong in a note
Because negative results bound the scope and stop others from repeating the same checks, or tell them precisely which checks to extend
blocks.explain: "No other host contacted the IP in 7 days of proxy logs" is a scope boundary. Without it, IR either repeats the search or wrongly assumes it was done more broadly.

lessons.title: Talking to users, owners and leaders during an investigation

blocks.md:
Analysts spend a surprising share of the day talking to people: a user who may have been phished, an owner whose server you want to isolate, an incident lead who needs a two-line summary, a manager who wants to know whether to worry. Four rules cover most of it.

**1. Use a channel the attacker cannot control.** If an account may be compromised, its mail, chat and even its phone number (after a SIM swap) may be in the attacker's hands. Contact people through a number from the HR record or in person. Ron Plesco, a cybercrime lawyer at the firm DLA Piper, told NPR about investigations where attackers were "watching your email, they're compromising your phone calls or your Zooms" while defenders planned their response.

**2. No blame, ever.** The user who clicked is your best witness, and the next one to report a phish. The NCSC warns that blaming or punishing people for clicking does not work and stops them reporting mistakes. Say what happened, what you did, what they need to do, and thank them.

**3. Write for the audience.** A system owner needs actions and impact on their system; an incident lead needs scope and confidence; leadership needs impact, decisions and when they will hear next. Start every update with the bottom line, separate known from unknown, and give the time of the next update even if nothing changes.

**4. Mind who may hear it.** The NCSC notes that insider threat work is sensitive and should be segregated from routine monitoring. If the person you would normally call could be the suspect, do not call: go to the incident lead, HR and legal first.

Label what you share. The [Traffic Light Protocol](https://www.first.org/tlp/) (TLP), maintained by FIRST (the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams), uses traffic-light colours to mark how far information may travel: TLP:RED for named recipients only, TLP:AMBER+STRICT within the organisation, TLP:AMBER within the organisation and its clients on a need-to-know basis, TLP:GREEN within a community, TLP:CLEAR for anyone.

blocks.code:
# Call script (to the number in the HR record, never one the alert supplied)
"Hi Ana, this is Sam from the security team. You can check this call
by phoning the IT service desk and asking for the SOC. We saw a
sign-in to your account at 09:41 UTC today from a device we do not
recognise. Was that you?  [listen]  Thanks. Nothing you did is a
problem; you helped by answering. We have signed your account out
everywhere and you will need a new password. Please do not approve
any sign-in prompt you did not start. We will call again by 14:00."

# Stakeholder update (to incident lead and leadership)  TLP:AMBER+STRICT
BOTTOM LINE: One Finance laptop and one account compromised via a
  malicious attachment at 09:15 UTC. Contained at 09:55. No evidence yet
  of data leaving; account access review in progress.
KNOWN: ...      UNKNOWN: ...      DECISION NEEDED: none / <decision>
NEXT UPDATE: 14:00 UTC, or sooner if scope changes.
blocks.caption: Two templates: a call script for the user, and a stakeholder update. Both say what is known, what was done, what is needed and when the next contact will be.

blocks.title: Who hears what, and when, during case C-312 (synthetic)

scenes.caption: 10:02. The analyst calls the user on the HR-listed number, explains how to verify the call, and asks one clear question. The user confirms they opened the invoice and did not sign in at 09:41.
10:05. Escalation with the case note. The incident lead declares an incident and takes ownership; the SOC keeps watching for the indicators.
10:20. The system owner (end-user IT) hears what was done to the laptop and why: isolated, not wiped, because IR needs the evidence.
11:00. The incident lead, not the analyst, briefs leadership: bottom line, known and unknown, decisions needed, next update at 14:00.
Afterwards the analyst closes the loop with the user: what happened, that they helped, and what to watch for. That conversation is what makes the next report come in early.

blocks.md: **Real communication under pressure.** Colonial Pipeline's CEO told the Senate the company "proactively reached out" to the FBI on the morning of the attack, scheduled a debrief call with the FBI and CISA within hours, and shared indicators of compromise with law enforcement. Uber published a plain-language security update within days: what happened, how it responded, what the impact was, who it believed was responsible. Neither knew everything when it spoke; both said what they knew and what they were still checking. That is the pattern for every internal update an analyst writes too.

Never let an attacker-controlled message decide who you trust. A chat message saying "I'm from IT, please approve the prompt" is exactly what the Lapsus$ actors sent, per the CSRB. The same rule applies inside the SOC: verify urgent requests to disable monitoring or grant access through a second channel.

blocks.question: You suspect an employee is copying customer data to a personal cloud account. Who do you contact first?
options: The employee, to hear their side
Their manager, by email
The incident lead and, through them, HR and legal, keeping the case need-to-know
The whole security team channel
blocks.explain: Possible insider cases are sensitive: contacting the employee or a wide channel can tip them off, harm an innocent person, or break legal process. The NCSC advises segregating insider threat work for exactly these reasons.

blocks.question: Which first line suits an update to leadership at hour two of an incident?
options: "We have run 140 queries across 6 data sources."
"Attack by a sophisticated nation-state."
"One laptop and one account compromised; contained; no evidence yet of data loss; next update 14:00 UTC."
"Too early to say anything."
blocks.explain: Bottom line first: impact, containment status, what is still unknown, when they will hear next. Activity counts tell leaders nothing, unsupported attribution misleads, and silence breeds rumours.

lessons.title: SOAR playbooks: what to automate and what to keep human

blocks.md:
A **playbook** is the agreed sequence of steps for a kind of alert or incident; a **runbook** usually means the detailed, step-by-step instructions for one task. **SOAR** (security orchestration, automation and response) platforms run playbooks as code: *orchestration* means connecting tools through their APIs (the SIEM, the EDR, the identity provider, the ticketing system), *automation* means running steps without a person, *response* means taking actions such as revoking a session.

The pressure to automate is real. In the SOUPS 2015 study, analysts sent hundreds of near-identical "please re-image your device" emails by hand every day, with only the username and hostname changing, until an L2 analyst scripted it in their own time. The authors found automation happened through *reflection*, periodically reviewing procedures for repetitive steps, and that it freed skilled analysts for "more sophisticated investigations". Python for security covered how to write such scripts safely; this lesson is about what they should and should not do.

The NCSC calls runbooks "a contentious subject": scripted steps can "limit the level of genuine investigation", yet guidance on "which log sources to examine, which systems to investigate and who to contact" is extremely useful. A practical split:

**Automate** what is repetitive, fast and safe to repeat: enrichment (lesson 5), de-duplication, opening tickets (NIST suggests automatic ticket creation for certain alerts), collecting evidence, notifying the right queue, and low-risk reversible actions on low-value targets.

**Keep a human** wherever judgement or impact is high: anything destructive or hard to undo, actions on executives, production servers or break-glass accounts (emergency admin accounts), verdicts on novel activity, and every conversation with a user. A good pattern is *the robot prepares, a human decides*: the playbook gathers evidence and proposes the containment steps, and an analyst approves them with one click.

blocks.code:
# Illustrative format, not any vendor's syntax
name: suspicious-mfa-push-storm
trigger:
  rule: mfa_push_storm          # 5+ denied or ignored pushes in 10 min
steps:
  - id: enrich
    action: lookup
    with: [identity, asset_owner, past_alerts_30d, ip_reputation]
  - id: open_case
    action: create_ticket
    with: {queue: soc-l1, severity: "{{ alert.severity }}"}
  - id: approved_after_storm
    action: branch
    if: "{{ alert.then_approved }}"
    then: contain
    else: ask_user
  - id: ask_user
    action: notify_user
    channel: phone_number_from_hr_record   # never reply in the same session
    template: did_you_try_to_sign_in
    timeout: 30m
    on_timeout: contain
    on_confirmed: record
  - id: contain
    action: require_approval      # a human decides; the robot prepares
    approver: soc-l2-on-call
    proposes:
      - revoke_sessions: "{{ alert.user }}"
      - reset_password: "{{ alert.user }}"
      - block_new_mfa_enrolment: "{{ alert.user }}"
    never_for: [break_glass_accounts]
  - id: record
    action: append_case_note
    always: true
blocks.caption: playbook.yaml: a push-storm playbook in an illustrative YAML format (not any vendor's syntax). Note the approval gate, the out-of-band channel and the never_for list.

blocks.title: The push-storm playbook running on two alerts

scenes.caption: Run 1: a push storm for ana.silva followed by an approval. The trigger fires and enrichment adds identity, owner, past alerts and IP reputation in seconds.
then_approved is true: skip asking and go straight to containment, because a session may already exist.
The playbook proposes: revoke sessions, reset the password, block new MFA enrolment. The on-call L2 analyst reviews the evidence and approves. The robot prepared, a human decided.
Every step, including the approval and who gave it, is appended to the case note automatically.
Run 2: a storm with no approval. The playbook phones the user via the HR-listed number. They answer: "I kept mistyping my password." The analyst closes it as benign with that note.
Run 3 would be a timeout: no answer in 30 minutes means containment is proposed anyway. Silence is not consent, and not proof of innocence either.

blocks.md:
Automation has its own failure modes, and an attacker can aim at them:

- **It acts on attacker-controlled input.** A playbook that auto-blocks any IP named in an alert can be tricked into blocking a partner's address or your own DNS resolver. Keep a never-block list and require approval for anything shared.
- **It inherits enrichment's lies.** Auto-closing on "benign reputation" closes the attacker on a CDN; auto-escalating on "malicious reputation" escalates last year's IP (lesson 5).
- **It fails silently.** An expired API key turns enrichment into empty fields. Alert on playbook errors like on any other log source going quiet.
- **It hides the reasoning.** If the playbook decides, the note must say what it checked and why.

For sharing playbooks between organisations and tools, OASIS (a standards body) publishes [CACAO](https://docs.oasis-open.org/cacao/security-playbooks/v2.0/security-playbooks-v2.0.html), Collaborative Automated Course of Action Operations, a JSON format for security playbooks.

blocks.question: Which step is the best candidate for full automation with no human approval?
options: Disabling the CEO's account on a push-storm alert
Isolating a production database server on an EDR alert
Adding identity, asset owner and past-alert context to every new identity alert
Closing alerts whose destination IP has a benign reputation
blocks.explain: Enrichment is repetitive, fast and harmless if it errs: it only adds context for a human. The others are high-impact (CEO account, production database) or rely on reputation data that is easily wrong (lesson 5).

blocks.question: A playbook automatically blocks at the firewall every source IP that triggers a brute-force alert. What is the main risk?
options: Attackers, or simple misconfigurations, can make it block addresses you depend on, such as shared carrier IPs or partners, turning your own automation into a denial of service
Firewalls cannot block IPs automatically
It makes the SOC too fast
Brute-force alerts are always false positives
blocks.explain: The trigger is driven by input others control, and IPs are shared (lesson 5). Bound the action: never-block lists, expiry times, approval for anything that is not clearly hostile and clearly yours to block.

lessons.title: Metrics, burnout and the analyst's ethics

blocks.md:
SOCs are measured, and the measures shape behaviour. The common ones, as defined in [Atlassian's incident management guide](https://www.atlassian.com/incident-management/kpis/common-metrics):

- **MTTA**, mean time to acknowledge: how long it takes to "recognize or respond to" an alert or incident.
- **MTTR**, which Atlassian notes can mean mean time to repair, recovery, resolve or respond. Always say which one, and where the clock starts and stops.

SOCs add their own: **false positive rate** (false positives divided by alerts closed), true positives found, alerts per analyst per shift. The script computes them for a synthetic week, and shows why a mean alone misleads.

blocks.code:
from statistics import mean, median

# SYNTHETIC: one week of closed alerts
# (minutes to acknowledge, minutes to close, verdict)
closed = [(2, 9, "fp"), (3, 12, "fp"), (3, 7, "btp"), (4, 15, "fp"),
          (5, 30, "tp"), (5, 11, "fp"), (6, 8, "btp"), (7, 14, "fp"),
          (8, 20, "fp"), (240, 300, "tp")]   # one alert sat over a weekend

tta = [a for a, _, _ in closed]
ttc = [c for _, c, _ in closed]
verdicts = [v for _, _, v in closed]
print(f"MTTA {mean(tta):.1f} min, median {median(tta)} min")
print(f"mean time to close {mean(ttc):.1f} min, median {median(ttc)} min")
fp_rate = verdicts.count("fp") / len(verdicts)
print(f"false positive rate {fp_rate:.0%}, true positives {verdicts.count('tp')}")

blocks.code:
MTTA 28.3 min, median 5.0 min
mean time to close 42.6 min, median 13.0 min
false positive rate 60%, true positives 2
blocks.caption: Output. One alert that sat over a weekend drags the MTTA from about 5 minutes to 28.

scenes.caption: Nine alerts acknowledged within 8 minutes. The tenth, a true positive, sat for 240 minutes over a weekend.
Mean 28.3 minutes, median 5. Neither number alone says the important thing: one true positive waited four hours. Report the median, a high percentile and the worst case for true positives.
Minutes to close for the same alerts: median 13, mean 42.6. The fast closes were mostly false positives. Speed is only good if the verdicts are right.

blocks.md: Metrics get gamed when people are judged on them. In the SOUPS study an L1 analyst said: "I think we are just working to generate numbers for higher management." A senior manager wanted something else: "If you tell me you processed some thousands of events over a month that does not tell anything interesting to me", but a case that led to new detections would. Good SOC reporting pairs a few numbers (median time to acknowledge true positives, false positive rate per rule, coverage gaps) with short stories of what was found and what improved.

**Burnout.** The same study models burnout as a vicious cycle between four parts of what the authors call *human capital*: skills, empowerment, creativity and growth. Low-skilled hires get little trust, so they are not empowered; without empowerment they cannot be creative, so they do not grow, so they stay low-skilled. Repetitive work with no reflection "exhausts the analysts". The study's remedies: empower analysts gradually, automate repetitive work through reflection, and choose metrics that reflect real value. The NCSC adds rotation across intelligence, rule writing and incident handling to avoid "triage fatigue".

**Ethics: the access you hold.** A SOC can read mail metadata, browsing logs, sign-in locations and file activity for everyone. The NCSC's SOC guidance expects requests like "Can you tell me what employee x was doing all day" and says answering "might not fall within the remit of the security operations centre". It suggests operating principles such as: work within the law, regulation and policy; collect or search sensitive data "only ... in order to detect malicious, suspicious or abusive behaviour"; keep data only as long as needed.

In practice:

- **Least access**: query only what the case needs, and only for cases you are assigned to.
- **Purpose**: curiosity about a colleague, a celebrity customer or a manager's request outside a formal process is never a reason to look.
- **Accountability**: your own queries should be logged and reviewable, just like the users you watch. The NCSC also recommends that SOC services sit in a separate security domain, so a compromised admin cannot quietly edit the audit trail.
- **Discretion**: what you see in an investigation stays need-to-know.

The analyst's job, in one sentence: answer each alert with evidence, quickly and in order of risk, write it down so others can act and check, and use the access that makes this possible only for that purpose.

**Practice legally.** These free or freemium platforms let you triage realistic alerts in safe labs: [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/) (investigations for defenders, free and paid tiers), [LetsDefend](https://letsdefend.io/) (investigating attacks inside a simulated SOC), [CyberDefenders](https://cyberdefenders.org/) (blue team labs for SOC work and DFIR, digital forensics and incident response), and [TryHackMe](https://tryhackme.com/) (its SOC Level 1 learning path). Pair each lab with this course's habits: the four triage questions, UTC timelines, a written case note for every verdict.

blocks.question: Your SOC's MTTA improved from 20 to 6 minutes after a new rule let analysts bulk-close alerts from noisy rules. What should you check before celebrating?
options: Nothing; faster is better
Whether true positives are still being found and how fast they were acknowledged, and whether bulk closures carry reasons that quality review can check
Whether the analysts are working longer hours
Whether the SIEM clock is correct
blocks.explain: Speed can improve by doing less looking. The metric that matters is how quickly real attacks were caught, and whether closures are still evidence-based. That is the gaming risk the SOUPS study describes.

blocks.question: A manager asks you to pull a list of websites their employee visited last week "to check if they're working". There is no case number. What do you do?
options: Run the query; managers can see their team's data
Run it but only share the top ten sites
Ask the employee for permission first
Decline and point them to the formal process (HR and legal), because the SOC's access exists to detect malicious or abusive behaviour, not for performance monitoring outside a sanctioned process
blocks.explain: This is the NCSC's example almost word for word. Monitoring for performance is a separate, policy-governed matter; using SOC access for it outside that process breaches least access and purpose limits.
